This meant that a great body of knowledge was now within reach of the Arabs, if they wished to draw from it.

But at first, we are told, the Muslims rejected these cultures and turned away from them, apart from a few rare exceptions. They were proud of their religion and unwilling to become students of peoples who had become their subjects. They did not seriously turn toward those cultures until changing circumstances brought them down from their former position of dominance.
There is more than one problem here from the standpoint of scientific method.
Before we even reach the question of method, there is a historical problem.

The claim that the Arabs “rejected” these cultures and “turned away from them except in a few rare cases,” and that they “did not turn toward them until changing circumstances brought them down from their position of dominance,” is contradicted by the historical evidence itself.
The historical sources give us no shortage of evidence to the contrary.
Even the works of Muslim historians and researchers, both older and modern, tell a different story.
They describe in great detail—sometimes even exaggerating—the many religious and philosophical ideas that entered from outside.
These ideas did not merely become part of Arab-Islamic culture. They also entered into the very disputes and conflicts that helped form some of the central structures of that culture.

Where rejection did occur, it was not a rejection of foreign cultures simply because they were foreign, or because they belonged to peoples who had “become subjects” of the Arabs, supposedly because the Arabs were too “proud of their religion” to become students of such “subjects.”
Nor did “the Arabs” as a whole, as one people or nation, reject these cultures in the way Ghurāba’s account seems to suggest.
Rejection came from particular groups, particular schools, or particular movements. It was one expression of wider social, intellectual, and ideological struggles.
Some ideas were rejected and others accepted.
Every act of rejection stood beside an act of acceptance.

But neither rejection nor acceptance was ever based simply on whether an idea was foreign. Ideas were accepted or rejected because they agreed or disagreed with the intellectual and ideological positions of the people considering them.
The second is that it is historically wrong to say that the Arabs did not seriously engage with foreign cultures until “changing circumstances brought them down from their position of dominance.”
The historical record shows that interaction with these cultures had already begun in the early Umayyad period.
It then became a powerful current during part of the early Abbasid period, when Arab political dominance was at one of its highest points.
The methodological problem is that Ghurāba’s account contains two approaches that scientific method rejects.
The first is a racially arrogant view of non-Arab peoples and their cultures.

This appears in the language of “tribal pride toward other peoples” and in the description of those peoples as “subjects.” Both expressions carry traces of an ideology of despotic domination and of class and racial superiority.
The second problem is the way cultural exchange is treated as something simple and mechanical on the one hand, and as a matter of personal choice on the other.
Once the Arabs had this “great body of knowledge” within reach, was the whole matter really just a question of what they personally wanted?
If they had “wanted” to draw from it, they could have done so—but they supposedly “did not want” to, and therefore did not?
Can a researcher writing in the second third of the twentieth century really imagine that the relationship between cultures works in such a simple, mechanical, and voluntary way?
The form taken by the relationship between one culture and another is not decided by personal wishes.
It is determined by objective reality—above all, by how close or how different the social relations reflected in the two cultures are.
Cultural interaction develops on this basis.
And this process of interaction is what produces the particular relationship between the two cultures.
The result is always a new stage in the development of both cultures.
But the decisive factor in shaping that new development is the internal dynamics of the culture doing the receiving, not the culture coming from outside.
This process of interaction has three main features.
First, it is complex, not simple.
Second, it is dialectical, not mechanical.
Third, it is objective, not subjective.
Acceptance and rejection are therefore not, at the deepest level, simple acts of accepting or rejecting something by conscious choice.
They are not voluntary acts of selection.
At their core, they are the result of ideas being absorbed and transformed from within.
Ultimately, they are the result of a complex, objective, dialectical process.

On the relationship between religion and philosophy, another book appeared after Ghurāba’s. Its title, The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy, seems at first to promise a new view of that relationship.
One might expect it to reach the underlying basis of the long-running conflict between religion and philosophy.

But the author describes the different forms this conflict took across the histories of Christianity and Islam, in Europe and in the East, from a secondary angle that remains far from the heart of the problem.
The main feature of his approach is the idea of reconciliation.
He begins from the unity of “truth,” which in the end means the truth of faith. Philosophical truth is therefore assumed to agree necessarily with religious truth.

From this traditionalist starting point, the history of the conflict between religion and philosophy can appear only as a series of different attempts to “reconcile” the two, with the form of reconciliation changing according to the religion, philosophy, and historical period involved.
Muslim philosophers, on this view, had to believe that religion and philosophy had the same aim and dealt with the same subjects.
They therefore had to make the attempt that supposedly gave Arab philosophy its distinctive character: the attempt to reconcile religion and philosophy.
But how do modern traditionalists understand this attempt?
The author of The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy gives us a clear example.
“reconciles religion and philosophy by interpreting religious verses in a way that makes their meaning agree with Aristotle (...) In other words, Ibn Rushd made religion submit to philosophy.”
“was no less enthusiastic than Saint Thomas in supporting the ideal that reason and faith are in harmony.”
He also says that Ibn Rushd tried to answer al-Ghazālī on the questions for which al-Ghazālī had declared the philosophers unbelievers, but that “reconciliation escaped him in this attempt.”

Taken together or separately, they produce a confused picture of “reconciliation.” But at the same time, they reveal that what the Muslim philosophers were actually trying to do was something other than reconciliation.
The first contradiction is between making religion submit to philosophy and being “enthusiastic for the ideal that reason and faith are in harmony.”
If religion is made to submit to philosophy, then there is no such “harmony.” Otherwise, why would one need to submit to the other?
The appeal to the interpretation of religious verses does not solve the problem.

In the history of Arab-Islamic thought, interpretation was often used by sects, schools, and intellectual movements as a way of hiding conclusions they did not dare state openly—especially their awareness that their own ideas conflicted with the apparent meaning of religious texts.
Different schools held different ideas, principles, and ideologies, and so they also developed different standards and methods of interpretation.
There was no single standard, no single method, and no universal rule governing interpretation.
The standard was often subjective or specific to a particular school.
Each legal, theological, doctrinal, or philosophical school might establish its own rules for how interpretation should be carried out.
Among extremist sects and philosophical schools in particular, interpretation was often a way to avoid openly confronting a conflict between their own ideas and the content of religious texts.
It was never, by itself, proof that their ideas were in “harmony” with those texts.
The second contradiction appears in the claim that Ibn Rushd tried to answer al-Ghazālī on the questions for which he had condemned the philosophers, but that “reconciliation escaped him.”
If making religion submit to philosophy really agreed with the supposed “harmony” between reason and faith, Ibn Rushd should have had little difficulty succeeding in this attempt.
But “reconciliation escaped him” because he could not in fact create a “harmony” that had no basis either in his philosophical system or in his ideological starting point.
Third, making religion submit to philosophy and reconciling religion with philosophy cannot be placed on the same level.
Submission means committing oneself to one side—in this case, philosophy—rather than the other, religion.
Reconciliation means committing oneself to both sides, religion and philosophy.

So if Ibn Rushd and the earlier “philosophers of Islam” really did make religion submit to philosophy—and this is in fact what they tried to do—then the “reconciliatory” character that modern traditionalist historians of philosophy, together with most Orientalists, have attached to Arab-Islamic philosophy is an illusion.
Modern Arab writers impose this character on the philosophy from particular social positions, just as many Orientalists do so from particular political positions.

The effect is to turn attention away from the real conflict between faith-based knowledge and rational knowledge, and away from the materialist tendencies contained in many of the conclusions reached by the “philosophers of Islam.”

The same starting point also lies behind the subjective or “ahistorical” explanations that modern traditionalists, and some other thinkers, give for the persecution of Muslim philosophers and philosophy.

For example, the author of The Story of the Conflict Between Religion and Philosophy also explains this persecution in terms of political and personal causes. The personal causes, he says, include “the envy scholars feel toward those among them who excel—that is, the philosophers; their resentment at seeing others become famous and widely known; their unease at the appearance of new ideas they are not used to; their attachment to old views they grew up with and came to believe were true (...) and, finally, the nature of religious belief itself. Faith often leads to dogmatism, and dogmatism cannot easily coexist with complete freedom of thought or with a willingness to accept whatever conclusions research and reflection may uncover.”

As for the political causes, we might expect the author to come closer here to the real logic of the problem. But that hope soon disappears, because he takes the argument in the opposite direction. By political causes, he means that rulers follow public opinion, accommodate the feelings of different groups, and adapt themselves to the outlook of the masses. Religious leaders, he says, may do the same in order to gain a good reputation among the people.
But looking at the political causes in this way turns the real logic of the problem upside down.

The problem has another logic: the logic of social and historical reality. When those rulers persecuted philosophy and philosophers, they were not simply following public opinion. They were acting in line with their own ideology as rulers in control of an autocratic, feudal system. Because of their position, they persecuted any form of thought that they believed might develop in a direction connected with the ideology of “public opinion” or “the masses”—even if this connection existed objectively and the philosophers themselves were not directly aware of it.

Persecution, then, was part of the normal pattern of rule under those caliphs and the groups attached to their governments. It was not a case of rulers being “carried along by public opinion” or adapting themselves to “the mentality of the masses.”

As for religious leaders, both the historical evidence and social analysis usually place them on the side toward which they were drawn by those in power. From that position, they in turn helped lead “public opinion” and “the mentality of the masses” in the same direction—not the other way around.
That is the real historical logic of the problem. It is very different from the picture presented by contemporary researchers who represent bourgeois thought.

Taha Hussein may have been trying to answer this common view of the persecution of free thought in Arab-Islamic history when he denied that Islam itself was the source of this persecution or the cause of hostility toward new ideas and freedom of opinion. He did so while defending freedom of thought, calling for renewal, and urging contemporary Arab thinkers to reject the old habits of intellectual stagnation.

Yet Taha Hussein began, in On Pre-Islamic Poetry, as a pioneer in studying the heritage through a historical method freed from traditionalism, only to end up a prisoner of traditionalism in much of what he wrote later.

Despite the dominance of the “ahistorical” method and subjective interpretation in modern studies of our philosophical heritage, we can still find, here and there, signs of a genuinely scientific approach to history. A few examples are worth mentioning.
